newsitem.title: USA: EIA's Hakes says economy fuels oil stocks decline.
newsitem.headline: EIA's Hakes says economy fuels oil stocks decline.

text.p: A sharp decline in the U.S. distilled oil product stocks this year has been fueled in large part by an unexpectedly strong economy, according to Jay Hakes, administrator of the Energy Information Agency.
"I think economic growth is truly a significant factor," Hakes told government agency and oil industry representatives at gathering here under the auspices of the New England Governors' Conference.
The decline in distillates, which comprise mainly heating oil, diesel and jet fuel, has given rise to fears that heating oil consumers may face sharp price increases this winter.

According to Tuesday's weekly report from the American Petroleum Institute, heating oil stocks in the northeast region, the world's largest market for the product, were at 24 millin barrels last week, or some 18 million barrels below last year's level.

"Most of the demand on any level will be met by production. Those production levels have been encouraging recently but what offsets that is the increasing demand from transportation," Hakes said. "The trucking business is very closely tied to economic growth."

Airline traffic also is up and jet fuel prices are up more than 40 pct in the last three months. As a result, British Airways said Tuesday that it would raise some European fares and consider raising others, while AMR Corp warned Wednesday that high jet fuel costs would depress fourth quarter earnings.

The Energy Department has said it won't intervene in the market and Hakes said on Wednesday that the government's decision to sell $220 million of crude oil from its Strategic Petroleum Reserve was already discounted by the market.

Energy Secretary Hazel O'Leary is due to meet oil industry executives on Friday in Washington to discuss the problem but she was warned on Friday by a leading consumer group that any collusion on prices might run afoul of U.S. antitrust laws.

"It is going to continue to be a volatile market througout the season." said Cheryl Trench, an analyst at Petroleum Industry Research Foundation who was attending the conference. "It isn't as though we are likely to suddenly build stock to the level that people are used to."

Hakes reiterated the EIA's forecast that heating oil prices could rise another nine to eighteen cents a gallon this winter, though Trench reckoned the higher end of that range is November heating oil futures in New York were at around 71 cents a gallon late Wednesday.
